opus-5.5.text:
I think mathematics is one of the most exciting areas, partly because of something specific to it: you can verify things. With formal systems like Lean, if a model produces a proof, you can check it mechanically. That gives you a clean reward signal, which is rare. In most domains, the hard part isn't generating candidates, it's knowing whether they're any good. In formal math, the verifier is essentially free and perfectly reliable, so you can let a model explore, fail a lot, and learn from what actually works.

That idea generalizes. The most promising areas are the ones where you can close the loop between generation and verification. In code, you have compilers and tests. In some parts of physics and chemistry, you have simulators that are decent proxies. Where you have that, you can do search plus learning, and things improve quickly. Where you don't, where every check means a months-long wet lab experiment, progress will be slower, and the value of AI there is more about prioritizing which experiments to run than replacing them.

I'm also fairly optimistic about AI as a research assistant in the broad sense: reading the literature, connecting results across subfields that rarely talk to each other, catching errors, filling in the tedious parts of a proof or derivation. A lot of science is bottlenecked not on the big creative leap but on a huge amount of careful, unglamorous work, and models are getting good at exactly that.

The longer-term question is whether these systems can come up with genuinely new ideas, not just solve problems humans posed. I don't think we're there yet, but the path probably runs through domains like math first, because that's where we can rigorously measure whether a model really did something new and correct, rather than just something that sounds plausible.

r001.rationale: The response names areas such as formal math, code, and parts of physics and chemistry, but does not identify domains where AI has not yet been applied as sources of readily achievable gains.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss domain specialists’ awareness of AI capabilities as a barrier.

r003.rationale: It does not propose pairing domain specialists with AI researchers to identify applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the most promising opportunities are the ones where we can get a fast, cheap verification signal. That's what made math such a natural first target for me. When I worked on theorem proving with Lean, the appeal wasn't that math is the most important science. It's that a proof checker gives you a perfect reward. The model proposes a step, Lean says yes or no, and you can run that loop millions of times without a human in the middle. That's the same structure that made Go tractable, and it's what lets you bootstrap from a weak model to a strong one.

So when I look at science more broadly, I ask: where does that loop exist, or where can we build it? Code is the obvious next one, because you have tests and compilers. Then there's anything with a reliable simulator. Protein structure, parts of chemistry, some physics. The simulator becomes your verifier, and the model becomes a search engine over hypotheses.

The harder but more interesting frontier is where verification requires the physical world. Running a wet lab experiment is slow and expensive, so you can't just hammer the loop. There I think the near-term value is less about the model discovering things alone and more about compressing the researcher's time. Reading the literature, proposing candidates, writing the analysis code, catching mistakes. Models are already very good at that, and open-weight models in particular mean a lab can run them on their own data without shipping it anywhere.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming a model that writes a nice paragraph about biology understands biology. We saw this in math. Language models were fluent about proofs long before they could produce correct ones. The gap closes when you connect the model to a verifier and let it fail a lot. So my bet is that scientific progress from AI will come field by field, in roughly the order in which we can make the feedback signal automatic.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is a particularly promising area, because you can verify whether an answer is correct. If you work in a formal system, you can generate a proof and have a proof checker tell you whether it’s valid. That gives you a very useful feedback signal for training models, without needing a human to evaluate every answer.

The exciting question is whether you can go beyond solving existing problems and help mathematicians discover something new—suggest a useful lemma, explore an approach, or make a connection that wasn’t obvious.

More broadly, I think there’s a lot of potential wherever you can connect a model to a reliable experiment or simulator. Generating plausible scientific ideas is one part of the problem. Being able to test them and learn from the results is what makes the process really powerful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think some of the most promising opportunities are in mathematics and in areas where you can verify whether an answer is correct. In mathematics, for example, if a model proposes a proof, you can use a formal system to check it. That gives you a much stronger learning signal than simply asking another model whether the reasoning looks convincing.

The exciting next step is to move from solving problems we already know how to solve to helping researchers explore: suggesting a conjecture, finding a counterexample, or identifying a useful intermediate result. You don’t necessarily need a system that does the entire research process autonomously. A tool that helps a scientist get past one difficult step could already be very valuable.

And I think the same principle applies more broadly: look for fields where models can propose ideas and there is a reliable way to test them, through computation, simulation, or experiments. That feedback loop is where I would expect a lot of progress.
